newsitem.title: Zaire: New Zaire PM has to deal with war, bankrupt state.
newsitem.headline: New Zaire PM has to deal with war, bankrupt state.

text.p: Zaire's opposition firebrand Etienne Tshisekedi has been handed back his former job as prime minister but he could be tested to breaking point by a widening civil war and all the problems of a bankrupt state.
President Mobutu Sese Seko agreed on Wednesday to name his arch-foe to the post from which he sacked Tshisekedi in 1993. Parliament nominated Tshisekedi the previous day.
"The decree has been signed," Mobutu's spokesman Kabuya Lumuna told Reuters after state radio announced the appointment.

Constitutionally, Mobutu was simply charged with signing an endorsement after an overwhelming majority of the opposition alliance in parliament and then Mobutu's camp adopted Tshisekedi as prime minister to replace disgraced Kengo wa Dondo.
Parliament voted two weeks ago to oust Kengo, a part-Tutsi widely accused of weakness in dealing with a rebellion spearheaded by ethnic Tutsis.
Mobutu has named a seven-member commission to attend weekend negotiations in South Africa with the rebel movement led by Laurent Kabila.

Banyamulenge Tutsis initially took up arms in October to fight attempts by local authorities to expel them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda. The rebel fold has expanded to include other Mobutu opponents determined to topple him.
Tshisekedi's entourage are under no illusion about the difficult task facing their leader. But they said on Wednesday night Tshisekedi would accept the post.

Aside from attempting to halt the relentless advances by the rebels who have seized a quarter of Zaire's territory and are now targeting its mainstay mining centres, Tshisekedi will inherit all the problems of a nation in economic ruin.
The prospects of him paying huge civil service salary arrears and keeping up payments to the army look slim.
In the streets of Kinshasa there was little of the celebration that might have been expected after Tshisekedi's long awaited nomination as prime minister.
As Mobutu's long-term political enemy, he commands huge popular support in the teeming slums of the capital.
He is widely viewed as the one political leader who has consistently stood up to Mobutu, in power since 1965, and argued for the creation of a state of law and democracy in Zaire.
"He is a man of the people, he acts for the well being of the people and not to fill his own pocket," said Papa Masamba, a refrigerator repairman.
But many of his most fervent supporters believe he will be accepting a poisoned chalice if he takes on the post of prime minister during the current crisis.
Militants of the radical opposition who meet on street corners in Kinshasa and are known as the "standing parliament" are against him accepting the post if it means serving under Mobutu.

"First of all we want Mobutu to resign. Mobutu has violated all the laws of the land. He will make sure that Kabila continues to fight against Tshisekedi," said 35-year-old Jean Pierre Mbambu, a militant Tshisekedi follower.
The rebels have taken an aggressive line against the civilian opposition in Zaire, saying they will not cooperate with any former collaborators of the president.
Radical opposition politicians who staunchly support the rebellion believe that if Tshisekedi accepts the post it will slow down the demise of the Mobutu era.
While many Zaireans hope he can entice Kabila into meaningful negotiations, the aggressive stance taken by the rebels towards him has left many doubting.
Some politicians say if he accepts the appointment as Mobutu's prime minister, it may be precisely because Kabila has threatened to exclude him from future transitional arrangements.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Wednesday he was hopeful the Zairean government and the rebels could set a date for a ceasefire during the talks in South Africa.
Answering questions from radio broadcasters in five continents, Annan said he expected both sides to agree on a date for both proper negotiations and a ceasefire.
He said he left an African summit in Lome, Togo, last week with the "understanding that the parties will accept a ceasefire and negotiations and that the date was to be announced later".
"I expect that the parties will agree to a date before the end of this week or not later than April 5," he said, adding that his special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun would then open the negotiations.
"So I would expect an announcement soon on a ceasefire and on commencement of talks," Annan said.
